title: 吧 and 呢
explain: 吧 softens a sentence. After a suggestion it means 'let's' or 'how about': 我们去吃饭吧。 It also makes a polite invitation gentler: 请坐吧 (Please, have a seat).
吧 can also check what you already think is true, like 'right?': 你没事吧？ (You are all right, aren't you?)
呢 asks 'and what about…?' by bouncing a question back: 我很好，你呢？ (I am fine, and you?)
呢 can also ask where something is: 你的手机呢？ (Where is your phone?)
mistakes: Use 吗 when you really want a yes/no answer. 吧 suggests or checks, 吗 asks.

q.explain: 吧 at the end makes it a suggestion.
呢 asks 'and you?'
Thing + 呢 asks where it is.

q.prompt: Which sentence says: Let's go to school?
q.explain: 吧 makes the suggestion.
吧 checks an assumption.

title: 在, 正在 and 呢: happening now
explain: Put 在 or 正在 before a verb to say it is happening right now: 爸爸在做饭。他正在看电视。
呢 at the end is optional and sounds lively: 他正在看书呢。 You can even use 呢 alone: 小明睡觉呢。
Be careful: 在 + place means 'at' (我在家), and 在 + verb means 'in the middle of' (我在看书).
For habits, use the plain verb: 我早上喝茶 (I drink tea in the morning). Putting 在 in front, 我在喝茶, changes the meaning to 'right now'.

examples.zh: 爸爸在做饭，妈妈在看书。
examples.en: Dad is cooking and Mom is reading.
He is watching TV right now.
My older brother is reading right now.

mistakes: For a habit, use the plain verb: 我早上喝茶. 我在喝茶 would mean 'I am drinking tea right now'.

q.explain: 在 + verb is 'in the middle of'.

q.en: He is watching TV right now.
q.explain: 正在 stresses 'right now'.

q.en: My older brother is reading right now.
q.explain: 呢 can finish an in-progress sentence.

q.prompt: Which sentence says: Dad is cooking?
q.explain: 在 + verb is in progress. 爸爸在家 only says he is at home.

q.en: They are having class right now.
q.explain: 正在 goes before the verb.

title: 了 after a verb: it's done
explain: 了 right after a verb says the action is finished: 我买了一本书。 (I bought a book.)
It is not a past-tense marker. It marks 'completed'. Do not use it for habits (我早上喝茶, not 我早上喝了茶), although one particular morning is fine (我今天早上喝了茶), or for plain facts about a state (我昨天在家).
A short sentence like 我买了书 can sound unfinished. Add an amount or a describing word: 我买了一本书, 妈妈喝了一杯茶. Or put 了 at the end: 我买书了。
To say it did not happen, use 没(有) and drop 了: 我没买书。
Ask with 吗: 你吃饭了吗？

examples.en: Mom drank a cup of tea.
I did not buy a book.

mistakes: Do not add 了 to habits: 我早上喝茶 (not 我早上喝了茶). For one particular morning, 了 is fine: 我今天早上喝了茶.
Do not keep 了 in the negative: 我没买书 (not 我没买了书).

q.explain: 了 goes right after the verb.
了 marks a finished action.

q.prompt: Which sentence says: I did not buy a book?
q.en: I did not buy a book.
q.explain: With 没, drop 了.

q.prompt: Which sentence says: I drink tea in the morning (my habit)?
q.en: I drink tea in the morning.
q.explain: A habit does not take 了.
了 + 吗 asks whether it happened.

title: 了 at the end: something has changed
explain: 了 at the end of a sentence says 'now it is like this': a change or a new situation. 天冷了 means 'It has turned cold'. 下雨了 means 'It is raining now'. 我八岁了 means 'I am eight now'.
A sentence like this does not need a subject: 下雨了！ 下课了！
Compare 今天很冷 (a plain fact, it is cold today) with 天冷了 (news: it has turned cold).
太…了 is a separate pattern: 太好了！ (That is great!)

examples.en: Class is over, let's go and eat.

q.explain: 了 at the end shows a change.
了 marks the new situation.

q.prompt: Which sentence says: It has turned cold?
q.explain: 了 shows it just changed. 天很冷 only describes how it is.
了 shows he has become ill.
了 at the end: it has just become eight.

title: 和 and 对
explain: 和 joins nouns and pronouns, like 'and': 我和爸爸, 老师和学生。 To link two whole sentences, use a comma instead.
With 都, put 都 after the whole group: 我和他都是学生。
对 + person + verb means 'to / toward someone': 他对我很好。我对他说：'你好！'
对 also means 'right, correct': 对，我是学生。

examples.en: Dad and I both like reading.
He is very nice to me.
Yes, that's right, I am a student.

mistakes: 都 comes after the group: 我和他都是学生, not 我都和他是学生.

q.en: The teacher and the students are all very happy.
q.explain: 都 comes after 老师和学生.
和 joins the two people.

q.en: He is very nice to me.
q.explain: 对 + person means 'toward'.

q.prompt: Which sentence says: He and I are both students?
q.en: He and I are both students.
q.explain: 都 goes after the whole group.

q.en: Dad and I both like reading.
q.explain: 和 joins the nouns, then 都 comes before the verb.

title: Two actions in a row, and giving
explain: Chinese lines up verbs in the order they happen: 我去商店买水果 means 'I go to the shop to buy fruit'. The second action is the purpose of the first.
Sometimes the first action is how you do the second: 爸爸开车去公司 (Dad drives to work), 我坐火车回家 (I take the train home).
Giving and asking can take two objects, the person first: 爸爸给小明一本书 (Dad gives Xiaoming a book). 我问老师一个问题 (I ask the teacher a question).
给 + person before a verb means 'for / to someone': 我给妈妈打电话 (I call my mom).

examples.en: I go to the shop to buy fruit.

mistakes: Keep the order of events: 我去商店买水果, not 我买水果去商店.

q.en: I go to the shop to buy fruit.
q.explain: 去 first, then the reason.
How you go comes first.
给 + person + thing.

q.en: I ask the teacher a question.
q.explain: 问 + person + thing.

q.prompt: Which sentence says: I call my mom?
q.explain: 给 + person goes before the verb.

title: 请, 一下 and 喂
explain: 请 + verb means 'please': 请坐。请喝茶。 请问 means 'may I ask…?' and opens a question: 请问，学校在哪儿？
Verb + 一下 means 'for a moment' or 'a little': 我问一下老师。我想休息一下。 It also makes a request softer.
喂 is how you answer or start a phone call: 喂，你好！ 喂，请问小明在家吗？
Some verbs already include an object (睡觉, 上课, 说话). Put 了 after the whole word: 他们上课了。 When another action follows, 了 may move inside: 下了课，我们去吃饭。

examples.en: Excuse me, where is the school?
I want to rest for a bit.

mistakes: 请 comes before the verb: 请坐, not 坐请.

q.en: Excuse me, where is the school?
q.explain: 请问 opens the question.
请 + verb is 'please'.

q.en: I want to rest for a bit.
q.explain: 一下 goes after the verb.

q.prompt: Which sentence says: I'll just ask the teacher?
q.explain: 一下 goes right after the verb.
喂 is how you answer the phone.

title: Some and a little: 一些, 一点儿, 有些, 有的, 有点儿
explain: 一些 means 'some' or 'a few' and goes before a noun: 我想买一些水果。
一点儿 means 'a little' or 'a bit' of something: 我会说一点儿汉语。
有些 and 有的 mean 'some (of them)' and start a sentence about part of a group: 有些学生不喜欢读书。有的人喜欢喝茶，有的人喜欢喝牛奶。
有点儿 is different. It goes before an adjective and means 'a bit', often about something you do not like: 今天有点儿冷。

examples.en: I want to buy some fruit.
I can speak a little Chinese.
It is a bit cold today.

mistakes: 有点儿 goes before an adjective: 今天有点儿冷. Say 我会说一点儿汉语 for 'a little Chinese'.

q.en: I want to buy some fruit.
q.explain: 一些 goes before the noun.

q.en: I can speak a little Chinese.
q.explain: 一点儿 means 'a little' of something.

q.en: It is a bit cold today.
q.explain: 有点儿 goes before an adjective.

q.prompt: Which sentence says: It is a bit cold today?
q.en: It is a bit cold today.
q.explain: Use 有点儿 before an adjective.
有的 + noun starts a statement about part of a group.
